parole.testo: Apparently from Turkic, whence also Kazakh абыржыған (abırjığan), Tatar аптыраган (aptırağan, “confused, bewildered”), аптырау (aptıraw, “mystify, be confused”), Chuvash аптӑрат (aptărat, “confuse, torment, frustrate”).

parole.significato: aimag (various historical or modern Turkic or Mongolian provinces)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic or Mongolian аймаг (ajmag). Cognates include Kyrgyz аймак (aymak), Kazakh аймақ (aymaq).
From a Turkic language; compare to Tatar әйрән (äyrän), Turkish ayran.

parole.significato: aqsaqal or aksakal (a village elder in some Central Asian cultures)
parole.testo: From Turkic languages, cognates include Tatar аксакал (aqsaqal), Kazakh ақсақал (aqsaqal) or Kyrgyz аксакал (aksakal).
From Old East Slavic алъ (alŭ, “bright red; crimson”), from a Turkic source. Compare Bashkir ал (al, “bright red”), Turkish al (“crimson”).

parole.significato: amanat (a hostage from a local tribe taken by Russian troops during reconnaissance or exploration, e.g. in Siberia duri…
parole.testo: Via a Turkic language from Arabic أَمَانَة (ʔamāna, “surety”).
Via Turkic (compare Tatar амбар (ambar)) from Persian انبار (anbâr).
Inherited from Old East Slavic арапъ (arapŭ), from Turkic; compare Turkish Arap (“Arab”).

parole.significato: araba (a horse- or bullock-drawn cart with two large wheels)
parole.testo: From a Turkic source. See araba for more.
Inherited from Old East Slavic арбузъ (arbuzŭ), via Turkic from Persian خربز (xarboz).
From a Turkic source. Compare Bashkir арҡан (arqan), Kazakh арқан (arqan).
From a Turkic source, such as Azerbaijani arxalıq.

parole.significato: aul (a type of village in the Caucasus or Central Asia)
parole.testo: From West (Kypchak) Turkic awul, awïl; related to Ottoman Turkish آغل (“penfold”). Compare Karachay-Balkar ауул (awul), Bashkir ауыл (awıl), Kazakh ауыл (awıl) and Turkish ağıl.
From a Turkic source, from Persian بازار (bâzâr, “market, bazaar”).

parole.significato: bay or bai, a rich man, lord, (by extension) exploiter
parole.testo: From a Turkic source. Cf Turkish bay, Azerbaijani bay, Kazakh бай (bay), Kyrgyz бай (bay), Tatar бай (bay), Bashkir бай (bay), Turkmen baý.

parole.significato: Eid, Bayram (a Muslim religious festival), abbreviation of курбан-байра́м (kurban-bajrám, “Eid al-Adha”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Turkic source. Compare Bashkir байрам (bayram), Tatar бәйрәм (bäyräm), Khakas пайрам (payram), Kazakh мейрам (meyram), Kyrgyz майрам (mayram), Azerbaijani bayram, Turkish bayram etc.

parole.significato: a type of flask for carrying liquids with hooks on the sides for straps
parole.testo: Uncertain. Attested since 16th century. May be from some Turkic language, compare Crimean Tatar bakla (“wooden measure for grain”). May be from some South Slavic language, compare Bulgarian бъ́кел (bắkel), бъ́клица (bắklica, “bottle”), Macedonian баклица (baklica, “water vessel”), Serbo-Croatian ба̏
From a Turkic language, compare Proto-Turkic *baltu (“axe”). Compare typologically дуби́на (dubína), оря́сина (orjásina).
From a Turkic source.
From a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bars, also related to Proto-Mongolic *bars. See Turkish pars, Kazakh барыс (barıs), Mongolian бар (bar), Dongxiang basi.

From a Turkic source (compare Turkish porsuk, Kazakh борсық (borsıq, “badger”)), from Proto-Turkic *borsuk (“badger”). Compare Ukrainian борсу́к (borsúk, “badger”). Displaced native язве́ц (jazvéc), from Proto-Slavic *jàzvьcь (“badger”).
Cognate with бары́ш (barýš, “profit”), a Turkic borrowing.

parole.significato: a garden/field/plantation for watermelons, melons or pumpkins
parole.testo: Via a Turkic source, borrowed from Persian باغچه (bâġče). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂g-. Compare typologically наде́л (nadél), уде́л (udél).

parole.significato: pate, noggin, bonce (slang word for head, part of the body)
parole.testo: From a Turkic language, probably a borrowing of a dative singular form attested in Kipchak languages; compare Tatar баш (baş, “head”), Bashkir башҡа (başqa, literally “head.SG.DAT”). Initial (in 17th century) meaning 'head of a large fish' implies an origin related to fish trade in South Russia (e.g
Originally used by Cossacks, likely of Turkic origin. Compare Tatar баш (baş). Also see башловка (bašlovka, “the top share of Cossacks' loot, given to the leader or bravest Cossack.”).
Borrowed from a Turkic source — compare Bashkir башлыҡ (başlıq, “piece of headwear”), Turkish başlık (“hat”)).
Borrowed from a Turkic source (perhaps Ottoman Turkish باشمق (başmak)), from Proto-Turkic *baĺmak (“boot, shoe”). Compare Tatar башмак (başmaq, “shoe”), dialectal Turkish başmak (“shoe”).
Via a Turkic language from Persian پیروزه (piruze). See فیروزه (firuze) for more.
Borrowed from a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bȫrü. Compare Kazakh бөрі (böri), Tatar бүре (büre).

parole.significato: Beetewk (a type of Russian heavy draft horse)
parole.testo: Named after Bityug river near Voronezh, ultimately from a Turkic source.

parole.significato: bogatyr, a medieval heroic warrior in Kievan Rus
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Russian богатꙑрь (bogatyrʹ), багатꙑрь (bagatyrʹ), from a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bagatur. First attested in Russian in 1425. Compare Ukrainian богати́р (bohatýr), Mongolian баатар (baatar), Bashkir батыр (batır), Turkish batur, Persian بهادر, etc. More at
From a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *buka, compare Uzbek buqa. Cognates include Ukrainian буга́й (buháj), Belarusian буга́й (buháj).
Borrowed from Turkic; compare Bashkir буран (buran), Crimean Tatar boran, Kazakh боран (boran), Kyrgyz бороон (boroon), Tatar буран (buran), etc.
A Turkic borrowing, from Turkish bardak (“jug, drinking vessel”).
A Turkic borrowing, to be compared with Tatar борындык (borındıq, “chipmunk”) or, less likely, a reshaping of Eastern Mari у́рымдо (úrymdo, “chipmunk”).

A post-Mongol invasion – attested first in the Praying of Daniel the Immured – Turkic borrowing of a form bōr or būr applied to bay horses, found in Chagatai بور (bōr, “bay horse”), ultimately of Iranian origin equivalent to Middle Persian [script needed] (bwl /⁠bōr⁠/, “reddish-brown, bay”), Persian
Borrowed from Turkic, from Arabic بَزّ (bazz), see more there.
волк (volk, “wolf”) + -о- (-o-) + дав(ить) (dav(itʹ), “to press”), possibly calqued from Turkic, compare Azerbaijani qurdbasar, Kazakh бөрібасар (böribasar, “wolfhound, lit. wolf-presser”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic юкъ (jukŭ, “burden, load”), From a Turkic source, from Proto-Turkic *yük (“load, burden, freight”). Influenced by вить (vitʹ) (since Old East Slavic вити (viti)).

From a Turkic source, cf. Kazakh теңге (teŋge), Bashkir тәңкә (täñkä) perhaps from the Russian дань. First used in the singular form де́ньга, деньга́ (dénʹga, denʹgá, “ancient coin”), preserved in modern Russian as деньга́ (denʹgá, “money, dough (colloquial)”).

parole.significato: dzhigit (djigit, jigit) (a skilled horseman in the Caucasus and Central Asia).
parole.testo: From Turkic. Cf. Karakalpak jigit, Kazakh жігіт (jigit), Kyrgyz жигит (jigit), Karachay-Balkar джигит (cigit), Southern Altai јиит (ǰiit), јигит (ǰigit), Shor чиңет (čiŋet), Khakas чиит (çiit) etc.

parole.significato: domra (round-bodied lute of East Slavic origin with either three or four strings)
parole.testo: From a Turkic language, from Persian تنبور (tanbur). Compare Kazakh домбыра (dombıra), Uzbek doʻmbira, Bashkir думбыра (dumbıra). Doublet of домбра́ (dombrá) and танбу́р (tanbúr).
Inherited from Old East Slavic евшанъ (jevšanŭ) (attested 1201), from a Turkic language; compare to Ottoman Turkish یاوشان, Turkish yavşan, Turkmen ýowşan.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Tatar аралаш (aralaş), Kazakh аралас (aralas). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *āra.

parole.significato: creek, brook, a secondary or intermittent river-channel
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic. Per Vasmer, from *yarïk (“crack, fracture”), compare Turkish yarık, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yār- (“to split”). However, more likely from *ayïrïk (“fork, crossroad, creek, brook”), particularly compare ablauted Tatar әйерек (äyyerek), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *adïr- (“
Via a Turkic language, ultimately from Middle Mongol 札撒兀勒 (zhásāwùlè /⁠⁠ǰasa'ul⁠/). Compare Ukrainian осавул (osavul, “Cossack captain”). Distantly related to яса́к (jasák).

Probably a Turkic or Mongolic borrowing. Compare Kazakh жез (jez, “brass”), Tatar җиз (ciz, “brass”), Mongolian зэс (zes, “copper, brass”). Remodeled under the influence of жесть (žestʹ, “frozen soil”).
A Turkic loan word. Cognate with Uyghur ئۈزۈم (üzüm, “grape”), Turkish üzüm.
From Turkic (compare Turkish incir), from Persian انجیر (anjir).
From a Turkic language, ultimately from Middle Mongol *ïrgaï. Compare Kazakh ырғай (ırğay, “juneberry”), Mongolian яргай (jargaj, “dogwood, cornel”).

Inherited from Middle Russian иша́къ (išák), ише́къ (išék), attested in 1567 and 1623. Further borrowed from Turkic languages, probably from Kipchak. Compare Tatar ишәк (işäk), Bashkir ишәк (işäk), also Turkish eşek, Crimean Tatar eşek, Azerbaijani eşşək), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *eĺčgek, which
A Turkic borrowing, compare to Azerbaijani qabaq (“pumpkin”), Tatar кабак (qabaq, “pumpkin”), Turkish kabak (“zucchini, squash”).
From a Turkic language, ultimately from Middle Mongol 合班; Compare Kazakh қабан (qaban), Tatar кабан (qaban), Azerbaijani qaban, Turkish kaban (dialectal) and others.

parole.significato: courgette, vegetable marrow, zucchini (an edible variety of Cucurbita pepo squash)
parole.testo: каба́к (kabák, “pumpkin”) + -ок (-ok, diminutive suffix), from Turkic; compare Azerbaijani qabaq (“pumpkin”), Tatar кабак (qabaq, “pumpkin”), Turkish kabak (“vegetable marrow; squash in general”).

Borrowed from Turkic, compare Kazakh қуырдақ (quwırdaq), ultimately derived from Proto-Turkic *kagur- (“to parch, to roast”). Sense 2 is the original one. For the development of the sense 1, compare каша (kaša, “porridge, mess”), винегрет (vinegret, “vinegret, mess”).

parole.significato: khagan (khan of khans; equal in status to an emperor)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic каганъ (kaganŭ), from a Turkic language, compare Old Turkic 𐰴𐰍𐰣 (k¹g¹n¹ /⁠qaɣan⁠/). Doublet of хан (xan).
A Turkic borrowing: compare Uyghur قاتتىق (qattiq, “hard”).

parole.significato: kazan (a type of cauldron or cooking pot used in Central Asian cuisine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Turkic language, compare to Azerbaijani qazan, Kazakh қазан (qazan), Turkish kazan, Uzbek qozon.

Related to казна́ (kazná). From a Turkic source, cognates include Tatar казначы (qaznaçı), Kazakh қазынашы (qazınašı), Kyrgyz казыначы (kazınacı), Uzbek xazinachi / gʻaznachi, Uyghur خەزىنىچى (xezinichi), Turkmen hazynaçy.
From a Turkic language.
Borrowed from a Turkic language, compare Kazakh қалта (qalta, “pouch, pocket”), from Persian خلته (xalta), خلیته (xalīta), from Arabic خَرِيطَة (ḵarīṭa).
From Turkic; compare Tatar камка (qamqa), Kazakh қамқа (qamqa, “silk fabric, similar to satin”). Ultimately from Persian کمخا (kamxâ).

Borrowed from a Turkic verb *qamla- (“to perform a shamanistic ritual”), affixed by -а́ть. Turkic source details The Turkic source verb *qamla- (“to perform a shamanistic ritual”) is derived from Proto-Turkic *kām (“shaman, sorcerer”) + action affix -la-. *Compare Old Turkic [script needed] (qamla-,
From Turkic. Compare Turkish kamış.

parole.significato: shackles, manacles, gyves, fetters, irons (paired wrist or ankle restraints)
parole.testo: Borrowed via Turkic from Arabic قَيْدَان (qaydān), dual form of قَيْد (qayd).

parole.significato: trap, bear trap, leg trap (device designed to catch or kill animals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Crimean Tatar qapqan and Turkish kapan (“trap, snare”). Cognate with Georgian ხაფანგი (xapangi, “trap”).
From a Turkic language. First attested in 1788.

Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkish karataş (“black slate”), from kara (“black”) + taş (“stone”), and Tatar кара таш (qara taş, “graphite, black lead”). The origin of the epenthetic -н- (-n-) is unclear. Compare каланча́ (kalančá) for the same epenthesis. First attested in the 16–17th c.
A Turkic borrowing; compare Tatar каравыл (qarawıl), Kazakh қарауыл (qarawıl). Ultimately from Middle Mongol ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯ (qaraɣul).
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Turkish karga. Compare typologically Latin striga, strix (< Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx)).
From earlier карый (karyj). Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kara.

Uncertain, a distorted word, with the р (r) presumably excrescent in compliance with Russian phonotactics, earlier гама́н (gamán, “purse, wallet”) which is still current usually in the extension гамане́ць (hamanécʹ) in Ukrainian; probably a Turkic borrowing, possibly with the Ukrainian and Southern

Attested since the middle of the 17th century. Related to кибита́ (kibitá, “arched hoop, half of a hoop of a large fish-trap”), obsolete (17th c.) киби́ть (kibítʹ, “arc of the bow”). Cognate with Ukrainian киби́тка (kybýtka), Belarusian кібі́тка (kibítka). Borrowed from Turkic: compare Tatar кибет (

A Turkic borrowing. Compare Nogai кынжал (kınjal), Kumyk хынжал (xınjal), Crimean Tatar къанджер (qancer), ханджер (hancer), гъанджер (ğancer), Tatar хәнҗәр (xäncär), Yakut кынчаал (kïnčaal). Related to Persian خنجر (xanjar).
Unclear. Likely from Turkic, compare: Turkish kürek, Azerbaijani kərki (“adze”) (whence Tat kerki). Compare also Ancient Greek κερκίς (kerkís).
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Kazakh кірпіш (kirpiš), Turkish kerpiç, Bashkir кирбес (kirbes), Azerbaijani kərpic, etc.
From a Turkic language, compare to Turkish kese, Azerbaijani kisə, from Persian کیسه (kise).
Borrowed from Turkic.

parole.significato: qishlaq, kishlak (a rural settlement of nomadic people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic, cognates include Turkish kışlak, Azerbaijani qışlaq.
Inherited from Old East Slavic *клобукъ (*klobukŭ), an early borrowing from a Turkic language. Cognate to колпа́к (kolpák).
From Turkic. Compare Turkish kubur.

parole.significato: high-crowned cap: cook cap, calpack, kalpak, fool's cap, nightcap etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic колпакъ (kolpakŭ), derived from a Turkic source. Compare Ukrainian ковпа́к (kovpák) or ковпи́к (kovpýk). Compare Bashkir ҡалпаҡ (qalpaq), Tatar калфак (qalfaq), Kazakh қалпақ (qalpaq), Uzbek qalpoq, Turkish kalpak (“cap”) etc. Ultimately from Middle Persian kwlʾp̄k' (k
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *karsak (“corsak fox”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic кочевати (kočevati), a Turkic borrowing, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *köč-. Contains the suffix -ева́ть (-evátʹ). Compare also Belarusian качаваць (kačavacʹ), Ukrainian кочувати (kočuvaty), Czech kočovat, Slovak kočovať, Polish koczować.
From a Turkic language. Compare Azerbaijani qoşmaq, Turkish koşmak.

Probably from Turkic, with the same meaning, from *kul (“hand”). Compare Bashkir ҡул (qul, “arm, hand”), Tatar кул (qul, “arm, hand”) and Turkish kol (“arm”). The sense of “wealthy farmer” is from the expression держа́ть в кулаке́ (deržátʹ v kulaké, “to keep in dependence”) or developed figuratively
Borrowed from Turkic; compare to Kazakh құм (qum), Kyrgyz кум (kum), Uzbek qum.
From a Turkic source, such as Tatar qımız (“fermented milk”).
From Turkic; compare Turkish kurgan (“fortress”).
Derived from Turkic.

Borrowed from a Turkic source. The Kipchaks themselves derived their name as meaning "hollow tree" (Karakhanid [script needed] (kuv) [script needed] (ağaç), from Proto-Turkic *ïgač (“tree”)). Compare Chagatay [script needed] (Qipčaq), Turkish Kıpçak. More at Kipchaks.

Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Chagatai [script needed] (alačuɣ) and Tatar алачык (alaçıq), Kyrgyz алачык (alacık), Crimean Tatar alaçıq, Azerbaijani alaçıq (“yurt”), meaning "felt tent", "shelter of branches"
Via Turkic (compare Turkish liman, Crimean Tatar liman) from Byzantine Greek λιμένιον (liménion), from Ancient Greek λιμήν (limḗn).

Inherited from Old East Slavic лошадь (lošadĭ), from лоша (loša), a Turkic borrowing; compare Tatar алаша (alaşa, “pack horse”), Chuvash лаша (laš̬a, “horse”), Kazakh алаша (alaša, “a kind of camel”), Crimean Tatar alaşa (“horse”), etc.

parole.significato: hinny (offspring of male horse and female donkey)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Turkic. See Russian ло́шадь (lóšadʹ).
From Turkic (Ottoman Turkish لوله (lüle)), ultimately from Persian لوله (lule).
Via Turkic from Arabic مَهْزُولَات f pl (mahzūlāt, “refuse, waste”), feminine plural of مَهْزُول (mahzūl). Influenced by ма́зать (mázatʹ).
From a Turkic language (compare Turkish meydan (“square”)), ultimately from Persian and Arabic مَيْدَان (maydān). The extended meanings are from Ukrainian майда́н (majdán).
From a Turkic language (compare Kazakh мешіт (mešit), Tatar мәчет (mäçet), Turkmen metjit), ultimately from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid).

parole.significato: target (butt or mark to shoot at)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic мишень (mišenĭ, “stamp, round plate, sign, tag”), from Turkic. Compare Turkish nişan.

Unknown. Attested since the first half of the 17th century. In view of мисю́рка (misjúrka, “a kind of helmet-armour with a net”), Ukrainian місю́рка (misjúrka, “a kind of helmet-armour with a net; glass-pearl”) apparently borrowed from a Turkic language which changes /b/ to /m/, doublet of би́сер (b

From Turkic (compare Tatar мөселман (möselman), Kazakh мұсылман (musılman)) + -ин (-in), ultimately from Classical Persian مُسَلْمَان (musalmān), from Arabic مُسْلِم (muslim). Doublet of басурма́нин (basurmánin).

parole.significato: muezzin (the man who issues the call to prayer)
parole.testo: Via a Turkic source, from Arabic مُؤَذِّن (muʔaḏḏin, “one who calls (to prayer), crier”).
From a Turkic source, from Persian نماز (namâz). Compare Kazakh, Kyrgyz намаз (namaz), Uzbek namoz, Bashkir намаҙ (namað), Turkish namaz.
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Kyrgyz нар (nar), Kazakh нар (nar).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Karaim otar (“pasture; flock of sheep”).
From a Turkic source; Kazakh ошақ (ošaq), compare Kyrgyz очок (ocok), Uzbek oʻchoq, Turkish ocak (“stove”); from Old Turkic očaq, očuq (“stove, oven”). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ōtčak (“hearth”).
From Turkic, ultimately from Middle Chinese 派 (pài, “to hand out, distribute”). Compare Turkish pay, Southern Altai пай (pay), Tatar пай (pay), Uzbek пай (pay).
Borrowed from Turkic, from Persian پلاس (pelâs).
Inherited from Old East Slavic печенѣгъ (pečeněgŭ), of Turkic origin and related to Turkish bacanak. Compare Hungarian besenyő.
From Turkic, from Persian رمضان (ramazân), from Arabic رَمَضَان (ramaḍān).

parole.significato: a large storage chest with a flat lid that could be used as a bench
parole.testo: A Turkic borrowing, Nogai орындыкъ (orındık”, “chair”), Kazakh орындық (orındıq, “chair”), Kyrgyz орундук (orunduk, “chair”), Tatar урындык (urındıq, “chair”).
Borrowed from a Turkic language. Ultimately from Middle Mongol ᠰᠠᠭᠠᠳᠠᠭ (saɣadaɣ, “quiver”); see Azerbaijani sadaq and Bashkir һаҙаҡ (haðaq) for more.
From Turkic. Compare Ottoman Turkish سازان (sazan).
Borrowed from a Turkic language. Possibly ultimately from Mongolic; see Azerbaijani sadaq and Bashkir һаҙаҡ (haðaq) for more.
From a Turkic language. See Turkish saman.
Via Turkic, from Persian سرای (sarây).
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *sārïg (“yellow”), compare Karakhanid [script needed] (sarïğča, “locust”).
According to Vasmer, a Turkic borrowing, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *siarïg (“yellow, white”).
From Turkic, such as Tatar söyrök (“sturgeon”) or Kumyk [script needed] (süyrik), both from Old Turkic *sivrüg (“sharpened, pointed”), referring to the snout. See also Turkish sivri (“sharp”).

parole.significato: the dogs bark, but the caravan goes on
parole.testo: Probably of Turkic origin, compare Turkish it ürür, kervan yürür.

parole.significato: the dogs bark, but the caravan goes on
parole.testo: Probably of Turkic origin, compare Turkish it ürür, kervan yürür.
Mid-17th century from a Turkic language which compounded the elements represented in Modern and Ottoman Turkish as صیر (sır, “varnish, glaze, enamel”) + ـغج (-gaç, -gıç, -geç, -giç).

Per Vasmer, there are two possible origins: # A borrowing from Turkic + -о́к (-ók); compare Kazakh суыр (suwır, “marmot”), Kyrgyz суур (suur, “marmot”), Chuvash сӑвӑр (săvăr, “marmot”). # Onomatopoetic, based on its characteristic whistle. In this case, it would be cognate with Latin sōrex (“shrew”)
From Turkic. Compare Turkish sürme, Azerbaijani sürmə, Crimean Tatar sürme, Tatar сөрмә (sörmä), Persian سرمه (sorme), from سرب (sorb, “lead”).

parole.significato: abomasum, maw, rennet-bag, the fourth compartment of the stomach of a ruminant
parole.testo: Related to synonymous Ukrainian сичу́г (syčúh), Belarusian сычу́г (syčúh). Usually considered a Turkic borrowing and compared to Kipchak suzug (“intestines”) (Codex Cumanicus), Chagatai [script needed] (sučuk, “stuffed intestines”), Ottoman Turkish صوجوق (sucuk, “sausage”). On the other hand, Trubač
Borrowing from a Turkic language; compare Ottoman Turkish طابور (tabur).
A Turkic borrowing: compare Tatar табын (tabın), Kazakh табын (tabın), Crimean Tatar tabın, dialectal Azerbaijani tabın. Akin to Georgian თაბუნი (tabuni), Armenian թաբուն (tʻabun).
Borrowed from Turkic, from Proto-Turkic *tugrag (“omen, sign, symbol”).

parole.significato: basin (a wide, relatively shallow vessel, e.g. for washing or cooking)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic тазъ (tazŭ), a Turkic borrowing. Compare Crimean Tatar tas, Turkish tas, Tatar тас (tas), etc. Ultimately from Persian تاس (tâs).
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *tal. Compare Kazakh тал (tal).
Derived from Old East Slavic тамъга (tamŭga), from a Turkic source (compare Bashkir тамға (tamğa) "brand, mark"). The suffix -ня (-nja) is intended to create nouns of place.

parole.significato: ulus, uls (various historical or modern Turkic or Mongolian regions)
parole.testo: From Turkic or Mongolic. Compare Mongolian улс (uls) / ᠤᠯᠤᠰ (ulus), Kazakh ұлыс (ulıs), Tatar олыс (olıs), etc.
From a Central Asian Turkic source. Compare Kazakh өрік (örik), Kyrgyz өрүк (örük), Uzbek oʻrik (“apricot”).

From a Turkic source, from Old Turkic ütüg, from Proto-Turkic *ütüg; whence also Turkish ütü (“iron”), Bulgarian ютия (jutija). Compare natively formed Czech žehlička (akin to жечь (žečʹ)), глачало (akin to гла́дить (gláditʹ)).
Via a Turkic source (compare Bashkir хаж (xaj), Turkish hac), from Arabic حَجّ (ḥajj).

parole.significato: dressing gown, bathrobe (for men or women)
parole.testo: A Turkic borrowing. Compare Ottoman Turkish خلعت (hilat, “kaftan”), Azerbaijani xələt (“dressing gown”), Uzbek xalat (“robe”). Ultimately from Arabic خِلْعَة (ḵilʕa, “robe of honor”).

Borrowed from a Turkic source. Compare Tatar чалма (çalma), Karachay-Balkar чалма (çalma), Turkish çalma.
A Turkic borrowing. See Ottoman Turkish كپنك (kepenek) for potentially pertinent forms.

Via a Turkic medium, from Persian جامهدان (jâme-dân, “suitcase”), from Persian جامه (whence also English pajamas, Russian пижа́ма (pižáma)). Note that this Russian term has later become the source of re-borrowing into modern Persian چمدان (čamedân) and many Turkic languages.

Of disputed origin, with suggestions including Turkic, Persian or Ancient Greek. The term became established in the 13th–15th centuries as a synonym for the older term зих (zix). From a Turkic language; compare Kazakh шұбар (šubar), Kyrgyz чыбар (cıbar), Bashkir сыбар (sıbar, “motley, speckled, spotted”).

parole.significato: gunny sack, burlap bag (a large sack holding 80–100 kg of grain or similar commodities)
parole.testo: A Turkic borrowing; compare to Azerbaijani çuval (“sack”), Tatar чувал (çuwal, “fireplace”).

Borrowed from Turkic whence modern Chuvash чӑваш (čăvaš, “Chuvash”), Tatar чуаш (çuwaş, “Chuvash”), and Eastern Mari суас (suas, “Tatar”). parole.significato: yurt (natural resources and arable land over which a Cossack stanitsa had exclusive control in their territory)
parole.testo: From a Turkic language, in the sense of referring to one's native land, from Proto-Turkic *yūrt (“dwelling place, camping site”). Doublet of ю́рта (júrta).
From a Turkic language, from Proto-Turkic *yūrt (“dwelling place, camping site”). Doublet of юрт (jurt).

parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ямьщикъ (jamĭščikŭ), from Turkic. Compare Tatar ямчы (yamçı), Turkish yamçı. Ultimately from Middle Mongol ᠵᠠᠮᠴᠢ (ǰamči) (see Mongolian зам (zam)). Ending modified under the influence of -щик (-ščik).
